claim: Cdh6 and Cdh8 are type II classic cadherins specific to sensory neurons in the mouse colon.
source: Our work identifies two type II classic cadherins, Cdh6 and Cdh8, specific to sensory neurons in the mouse colon.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cdh6+ neurons express Calcb and Nmu markers.
source: We show that Cdh6+ neurons demonstrate all other distinguishing classifications of enteric sensory neurons including marker expression of Calcb and Nmu, Dogiel type II morphology and AH-type electrophysiology and IH current.
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cdh6+ neurons have Dogiel type II morphology.
source: We show that Cdh6+ neurons demonstrate all other distinguishing classifications of enteric sensory neurons including marker expression of Calcb and Nmu, Dogiel type II morphology and AH-type electrophysiology and IH current.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cdh6+ neurons exhibit AH-type electrophysiology.
source: We show that Cdh6+ neurons demonstrate all other distinguishing classifications of enteric sensory neurons including marker expression of Calcb and Nmu, Dogiel type II morphology and AH-type electrophysiology and IH current.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings presented in Figure 3.

claim: Cdh6+ neurons exhibit IH current.
source: We show that Cdh6+ neurons demonstrate all other distinguishing classifications of enteric sensory neurons including marker expression of Calcb and Nmu, Dogiel type II morphology and AH-type electrophysiology and IH current.
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Cdh6+ sensory neurons in distal colon evokes retrograde colonic motor complexes (CMCs).
source: Optogenetic activation of Cdh6+ sensory neurons in distal colon evokes retrograde colonic motor complexes (CMCs), while pharmacologic blockade of rhythmicity-associated current IH disrupts the spontaneous generation of CMCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 6D-H.

claim: Pharmacologic blockade of IH current disrupts the spontaneous generation of CMCs.
source: Optogenetic activation of Cdh6+ sensory neurons in distal colon evokes retrograde colonic motor complexes (CMCs), while pharmacologic blockade of rhythmicity-associated current IH disrupts the spontaneous generation of CMCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments with ZD7288 and CsCl shown in Figure 6J-K.

claim: Cdh6 mRNA was expressed in 14.7 ± 0.8% of myenteric neurons in small intestine (jejunum).
source: Cdh6 mRNA was expressed in 14.7 ± 0.8% of myenteric neurons in small intestine (jejunum) and in 6.8 ± 0.3% of myenteric neurons in distal colon (mean ± SEM) (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Cdh6 mRNA was expressed in 6.8 ± 0.3% of myenteric neurons in distal colon.
source: Cdh6 mRNA was expressed in 14.7 ± 0.8% of myenteric neurons in small intestine (jejunum) and in 6.8 ± 0.3% of myenteric neurons in distal colon (mean ± SEM) (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Cdh8 was almost exclusively co-expressed in Cdh6+ neurons, although at a much lower level of detection.
source: Cdh8 was almost exclusively co-expressed in Cdh6+ neurons, although at a much lower level of detection (Figure 1D–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D-H.

claim: All Nmu+ neurons co-express Calcb in both jejunum and distal colon.
source: We found that all Nmu+ neurons co-express Calcb in both jejunum and distal colon (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Only about half of Calcb+ neurons in the jejunum co-express Nmu.
source: In contrast, only about half of Calcb+ neurons in the jejunum and two-thirds in the distal colon co-express Nmu (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Two-thirds of Calcb+ neurons in the distal colon co-express Nmu.
source: In contrast, only about half of Calcb+ neurons in the jejunum and two-thirds in the distal colon co-express Nmu (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Nearly all Nmu+ neurons in the jejunum express Cdh6.
source: In the jejunum, we found that nearly all Nmu+ neurons and Calcb+ neurons express Cdh6 (Figure 1P and U), though only about three-quarters of all Cdh6+ neurons express Calcb and only about half express Nmu (Figure 1O and T).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1P and U.

claim: Nearly all Calcb+ neurons in the jejunum express Cdh6.
source: In the jejunum, we found that nearly all Nmu+ neurons and Calcb+ neurons express Cdh6 (Figure 1P and U), though only about three-quarters of all Cdh6+ neurons express Calcb and only about half express Nmu (Figure 1O and T).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1P and U.

claim: About three-quarters of all Cdh6+ neurons in the jejunum express Calcb.
source: In the jejunum, we found that nearly all Nmu+ neurons and Calcb+ neurons express Cdh6 (Figure 1P and U), though only about three-quarters of all Cdh6+ neurons express Calcb and only about half express Nmu (Figure 1O and T).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1O and T.

claim: About half of Cdh6+ neurons in the jejunum express Nmu.
source: In the jejunum, we found that nearly all Nmu+ neurons and Calcb+ neurons express Cdh6 (Figure 1P and U), though only about three-quarters of all Cdh6+ neurons express Calcb and only about half express Nmu (Figure 1O and T).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1O and T.

claim: Cdh6 is only expressed in about two-thirds of all Calcb+ neurons in the distal colon.
source: In contrast, in the distal colon, while Cdh6 is only expressed in about two-thirds of all Calcb+ neurons (Figure 1U), nearly all Cdh6+ neurons express Nmu and Calcb (Figure 1O and T).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1U.

claim: Nearly all Cdh6+ neurons in the distal colon express Nmu and Calcb.
source: In contrast, in the distal colon, while Cdh6 is only expressed in about two-thirds of all Calcb+ neurons (Figure 1U), nearly all Cdh6+ neurons express Nmu and Calcb (Figure 1O and T).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1O and T.

claim: In the myenteric plexus, Cdh6 is expressed exclusively in Calcb+/Nmu+ IPANs in the mouse distal colon.
source: Taken together, our data show that in the myenteric plexus, Cdh6 is expressed exclusively in Calcb+/Nmu+ IPANs in the mouse distal colon (Figure 1W and X).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the marker colocalization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hb9:GFP+ neurons were rare and projected extensively throughout the myenteric plexus.
source: Hb9:GFP+ neurons were rare and projected extensively throughout the myenteric plexus (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: eGFP expression in Hb9:GFP mice was limited to a small fraction (3.5 ± 0.8%) of Cdh6+ colonic neurons.
source: In situ hybridization confirmed eGFP expression was limited to a small fraction (3.5 ± 0.8%) of Cdh6+ colonic neurons (Figure 2D and F–H), and all eGFP+ neurons expressed Cdh6 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D and F-H.

claim: All eGFP+ neurons in Hb9:GFP mice expressed Cdh6.
source: In situ hybridization confirmed eGFP expression was limited to a small fraction (3.5 ± 0.8%) of Cdh6+ colonic neurons (Figure 2D and F–H), and all eGFP+ neurons expressed Cdh6 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is quantified from RNAscope in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The membrane capacitance of Hb9:GFP+ colonic neurons was 32±8.7 pF.
source: Membrane capacitance reflecting overall size of these cells was 32±8.7 pF (Figure 3D); their resting membrane potential (RMP) was –49.4±2.9 mV (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The resting membrane potential (RMP) of Hb9:GFP+ colonic neurons was –49.4±2.9 mV.
source: Membrane capacitance reflecting overall size of these cells was 32±8.7 pF (Figure 3D); their resting membrane potential (RMP) was –49.4±2.9 mV (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The input resistance (Rin) of Hb9:GFP+ colonic neurons was 393±54.7 MΩ.
source: The input resistance (Rin) was 393±54.7 MΩ (Figure 3E) as computed from the slope of the voltage-current (V-I) relationship.
evidence: This is computed from voltage-current relationship data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: All patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons had large-amplitude action potentials (72±2.5 mV).
source: All patched neurons had large-amplitude AP (72±2.5 mV, Figure 3F and E) with threshold of –26.4±0.9 mV (Figure 3L) and a half-width of 1.2±0.1 ms (Figure 3H) elicited at rheobase (20±4.5 pA, Figure 3G), each followed by an afterhyperpolarization (AHP = –67.7 ± 0.9 mV, Figure 3K).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3F and E.

claim: The action potential threshold of Hb9:GFP+ neurons was –26.4±0.9 mV.
source: All patched neurons had large-amplitude AP (72±2.5 mV, Figure 3F and E) with threshold of –26.4±0.9 mV (Figure 3L) and a half-width of 1.2±0.1 ms (Figure 3H) elicited at rheobase (20±4.5 pA, Figure 3G), each followed by an afterhyperpolarization (AHP = –67.7 ± 0.9 mV, Figure 3K).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The action potential half-width of Hb9:GFP+ neurons was 1.2±0.1 ms.
source: All patched neurons had large-amplitude AP (72±2.5 mV, Figure 3F and E) with threshold of –26.4±0.9 mV (Figure 3L) and a half-width of 1.2±0.1 ms (Figure 3H) elicited at rheobase (20±4.5 pA, Figure 3G), each followed by an afterhyperpolarization (AHP = –67.7 ± 0.9 mV, Figure 3K).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The rheobase of Hb9:GFP+ neurons was 20±4.5 pA.
source: All patched neurons had large-amplitude AP (72±2.5 mV, Figure 3F and E) with threshold of –26.4±0.9 mV (Figure 3L) and a half-width of 1.2±0.1 ms (Figure 3H) elicited at rheobase (20±4.5 pA, Figure 3G), each followed by an afterhyperpolarization (AHP = –67.7 ± 0.9 mV, Figure 3K).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The afterhyperpolarization (AHP) of Hb9:GFP+ neurons was –67.7 ± 0.9 mV.
source: All patched neurons had large-amplitude AP (72±2.5 mV, Figure 3F and E) with threshold of –26.4±0.9 mV (Figure 3L) and a half-width of 1.2±0.1 ms (Figure 3H) elicited at rheobase (20±4.5 pA, Figure 3G), each followed by an afterhyperpolarization (AHP = –67.7 ± 0.9 mV, Figure 3K).
evidence: This is measured from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The first derivative of membrane voltage during the action potential (dV/dt) exhibited an inflection during the repolarization phase.
source: In addition, the first derivative of membrane voltage during the AP (dV/dt, Figure 3J) exhibited an inflection during the repolarization phase, suggesting the presence of fast and slow AP repolarization mechanisms (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is observed in the dV/dt traces shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The inflection in dV/dt during action potential repolarization suggests the presence of fast and slow AP repolarization mechanisms.
source: In addition, the first derivative of membrane voltage during the AP (dV/dt, Figure 3J) exhibited an inflection during the repolarization phase, suggesting the presence of fast and slow AP repolarization mechanisms (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dV/dt data shown in Figure 3J and F.

claim: Patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons generally could not sustain repetitive action potentials in response to long depolarizing current pulses.
source: Patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons generally could not sustain repetitive APs in response to long depolarizing current pulses.
evidence: This is observed from current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons responded to hyperpolarizing current pulses with a time-dependent membrane potential sag (–6.3±1.2 mV).
source: All patched neurons responded to hyperpolarizing current pulses with a time-dependent membrane potential sag (–6.3±1.2 mV, Figure 3B and M) and a rebound depolarization following the hyperpolarization (Figure 3B and N).
evidence: This is measured from current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3B and M.

claim: All patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons exhibited a rebound depolarization following hyperpolarization.
source: All patched neurons responded to hyperpolarizing current pulses with a time-dependent membrane potential sag (–6.3±1.2 mV, Figure 3B and M) and a rebound depolarization following the hyperpolarization (Figure 3B and N).
evidence: This is observed in current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3B and N.

claim: Voltage clamp step hyperpolarizations revealed IH (hyperpolarization-activated current) in Hb9:GFP+ neurons.
source: Consistent with these findings of sag and rebound, voltage clamp step hyperpolarizations revealed IH (hyperpolarization-activated current, Figure 3N) and, upon repolarization, IT (transient inward presumed Ca2+ current) (Huguenard, 1996) in terms of its kinetics (Figure 3O) and steady-state inactivation (Figure 3O and P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: Upon repolarization, IT (transient inward presumed Ca2+ current) was revealed in Hb9:GFP+ neurons.
source: Consistent with these findings of sag and rebound, voltage clamp step hyperpolarizations revealed IH (hyperpolarization-activated current, Figure 3N) and, upon repolarization, IT (transient inward presumed Ca2+ current) (Huguenard, 1996) in terms of its kinetics (Figure 3O) and steady-state inactivation (Figure 3O and P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 3O and P, with reference to Huguenard, 1996.

claim: Hb9:GFP+/Cdh6+ distal colonic neurons have action potential afterhyperpolarizing (AH)-type electrophysiology typical of IPANs.
source: Taken together, these results show that Hb9:GFP+/Cdh6+ distal colonic neurons have AP afterhyperpolarizing (AH)-type electrophysiology typical of IPANs, including rhythm generating currents IH and IT (Xiao et al., 2004; Nurgali et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3, with references to prior studies.

claim: IH and IT are rhythm generating currents in IPANs.
source: Taken together, these results show that Hb9:GFP+/Cdh6+ distal colonic neurons have AP afterhyperpolarizing (AH)-type electrophysiology typical of IPANs, including rhythm generating currents IH and IT (Xiao et al., 2004; Nurgali et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior studies (Xiao et al., 2004; Nurgali et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2006).

claim: Patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons displayed Dogiel type II morphology with large smooth cell somas and multiple branching neurites.
source: Patched Hb9:GFP+ neurons displayed Dogiel type II morphology (Furness et al., 2004), with large smooth cell somas and multiple branching neurites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biocytin-filled neuron tracings shown in Figure 4, with reference to Furness et al., 2004.

claim: Projections of Hb9:GFP+ neurons were mainly circumferential and extensively branched within myenteric ganglia.
source: Projections were mainly circumferential and extensively branched within myenteric ganglia.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biocytin-filled neuron tracings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hb9:GFP+ neurons display morphological features characteristic of IPANs.
source: Thus, Hb9:GFP+ neurons display morphological features characteristic of IPANs (Nurgali et al., 2004; Furness et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the morphological data shown in Figure 4, with references to prior studies.

claim: tdTomato+ labeling in Cdh6CreER;Ai14 mice represented about 5% of the total neuronal population in the myenteric plexus.
source: We confirmed tdTomato+ labeling in myenteric Cdh6+ neurons (Figure 5E and F), representing about 5% of the total neuronal population (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is quantified from imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons in Cdh6CreER;Ai14 mice had large cell somas with major axis 27.8±0.7 µm and minor axis 15.9±0.4 µm.
source: tdTomato+ neurons had large cell somas (major axis, 27.8±0.7 µm; minor axis, 15.9±0.4 µm) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is measured from imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: All ganglia of the myenteric plexus were densely innervated by tdTomato+ fibers in Cdh6CreER;Ai14 mice.
source: All ganglia of the myenteric plexus were densely innervated by tdTomato+ fibers (Figure 5A and B), which also projected into the circular muscle.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: tdTomato+ fibers in Cdh6CreER;Ai14 mice projected into the circular muscle.
source: All ganglia of the myenteric plexus were densely innervated by tdTomato+ fibers (Figure 5A and B), which also projected into the circular muscle.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Additional tdTomato+ labeling of some putative longitudinal and circular muscle cells was noted in Cdh6CreER;Ai14 mice.
source: We noted additional tdTomato+ labeling of some putative longitudinal and circular muscle cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is observed in imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: An IPAN array spans the entire motility circuitry of the colonic myenteric plexus.
source: Taken together, our data reveal an IPAN array that spans the entire motility circuitry of the colonic myenteric plexus.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In Cdh6CreER+;ChR2-eYFP+ colon preparations, spontaneous CMCs occurred at regular intervals of about 3–5 min.
source: In Cdh6CreER+;ChR2-eYFP+ colon preparations, we observed spontaneous CMCs at regular intervals of about 3–5 min.
evidence: This is observed in force recording data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Blue light stimulation of Cdh6+ IPANs in distal colon 60–90 s after a spontaneous CMC resulted in an evoked, premature CMC that began during stimulation.
source: Blue light stimulation of Cdh6+ IPANs in distal colon 60–90 s after a spontaneous CMC ('control' CMC) resulted in an evoked, premature CMC that began during stimulation (N=17 stimulations; n=5 mice) (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Evoked CMCs traveled retrogradely from the distal to the proximal colon.
source: Evoked CMCs traveled retrogradely from the distal to the proximal colon.
evidence: This is observed in force recording data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Evoked CMCs were similar to spontaneous CMCs in peak amplitude, area under the curve, and duration.
source: They were similar to spontaneous CMCs in peak amplitude, area under the curve, and duration, though the contractile force (peak amplitude and AUC) was slightly weaker in the proximal colon (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is quantified from force recording data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: The contractile force (peak amplitude and AUC) of evoked CMCs was slightly weaker in the proximal colon compared to spontaneous CMCs.
source: They were similar to spontaneous CMCs in peak amplitude, area under the curve, and duration, though the contractile force (peak amplitude and AUC) was slightly weaker in the proximal colon (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is quantified from force recording data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Blue light stimulation in proximal or mid colon failed to generate CMCs.
source: Blue light stimulation in proximal or mid colon failed to generate CMCs (n=5/5, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: Stimulation in control Cdh6CreER-negative;ChR2-eYFP+ colons failed to evoke any CMCs.
source: In comparison, stimulation in control Cdh6CreER-negative;ChR2-eYFP+ colons failed to evoke any CMCs (N=28 stimulations; n=7 mice) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spontaneous CMCs were abolished in hexamethonium.
source: Spontaneous CMCs were abolished in hexamethonium, and CMCs could not be evoked by optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6I.

claim: CMCs could not be evoked by optogenetic stimulation in the presence of hexamethonium.
source: Spontaneous CMCs were abolished in hexamethonium, and CMCs could not be evoked by optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Activation of Cdh6+ distal colon IPANs evokes retrograde-traveling but otherwise characteristic and hexamethonium-sensitive CMCs.
source: We conclude that activation of Cdh6+ distal colon IPANs evokes retrograde-traveling but otherwise characteristic and hexamethonium-sensitive CMCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic and pharmacological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Addition of 10 µM ZD7288 to the recording chamber abolished spontaneous CMCs.
source: Addition of 10 µM ZD7288 to the recording chamber abolished spontaneous CMCs and washout of ZD7288 recovered spontaneous CMC activity (Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Washout of ZD7288 recovered spontaneous CMC activity.
source: Addition of 10 µM ZD7288 to the recording chamber abolished spontaneous CMCs and washout of ZD7288 recovered spontaneous CMC activity (Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of 2 mM CsCl impaired or altered spontaneous rhythmic production of typical CMCs.
source: Addition of 2 mM CsCl also impaired or altered spontaneous rhythmic production of typical CMCs (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3); rhythmic contractions increased in frequency (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, 6/6), decreased in amplitude (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, n=4/6, p=0.0606), or in some cases even included significant retrograde force components (proximal colon, n=2/6; distal colon, n=2/6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: CsCl caused rhythmic contractions to increase in frequency in proximal colon (n=5/6) and distal colon (6/6).
source: Addition of 2 mM CsCl also impaired or altered spontaneous rhythmic production of typical CMCs (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3); rhythmic contractions increased in frequency (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, 6/6), decreased in amplitude (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, n=4/6, p=0.0606), or in some cases even included significant retrograde force components (proximal colon, n=2/6; distal colon, n=2/6).
evidence: This is quantified from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: CsCl caused rhythmic contractions to decrease in amplitude in proximal colon (n=5/6) and distal colon (n=4/6).
source: Addition of 2 mM CsCl also impaired or altered spontaneous rhythmic production of typical CMCs (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3); rhythmic contractions increased in frequency (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, 6/6), decreased in amplitude (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, n=4/6, p=0.0606), or in some cases even included significant retrograde force components (proximal colon, n=2/6; distal colon, n=2/6).
evidence: This is quantified from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: CsCl caused some cases to include significant retrograde force components in proximal colon (n=2/6) and distal colon (n=2/6).
source: Addition of 2 mM CsCl also impaired or altered spontaneous rhythmic production of typical CMCs (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3); rhythmic contractions increased in frequency (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, 6/6), decreased in amplitude (proximal colon, n=5/6; distal colon, n=4/6, p=0.0606), or in some cases even included significant retrograde force components (proximal colon, n=2/6; distal colon, n=2/6).
evidence: This is quantified from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pharmacologic blockade of IH in IPANs impairs the production of CMCs in the mouse colon.
source: We conclude that pharmacologic blockade of IH in IPANs impairs the production of CMCs in the mouse colon.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the pharmacological data shown in Figure 6J-K.

claim: In the small intestine, Cdh6 is also expressed in some Calcb+/Nmu- and Calcb-/Nmu- neurons.
source: Our study shows that in the myenteric plexus, Cdh6 is expressed exclusively in Calcb+/Nmu+ IPANs located in the mouse distal colon, while in the small intestine, Cdh6 is also expressed in some Calcb+/Nmu- and Calcb-/Nmu- neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cdh9 is exclusively expressed in the small intestine in mouse, not in the colon.
source: Notably, these markers show a different expression pattern than another cadherin, Cdh9, which is exclusively expressed in the small intestine in mouse, not in the colon (May-Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with reference to May-Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Cdh9 is expressed in a subset of IPANs not expressing either Calcb or Nmu.
source: Cdh9 is expressed in a subset of IPANs not expressing either Calcb or Nmu (Qu et al., 2008; May-Zhang et al., 2021; Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with references to Qu et al., 2008; May-Zhang et al., 2021; Morarach et al., 2021.

claim: Cdh6/Cdh8 IPANs are a separate population from Cdh9 IPANs.
source: We conclude that Cdh6/Cdh8 IPANs are a separate population from Cdh9 IPANs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNA-Seq data from two separate studies (Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021).

claim: IPANs are also present in the submucosal plexus.
source: Finally, our study was limited to the myenteric plexus, containing motility circuitry. IPANs are also present in the submucosal plexus, and it would be interesting to investigate Cdh6 expression and neuronal subtype in the SMP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Discussion section.

claim: CMCs can occur in the absence of luminal contents, without any apparent stimulus for IPANs to sense.
source: Though IPANs are positioned to initiate motility by activating other subtypes in enteric circuitry, their role in spontaneous CMCs has been debated, as CMCs can occur in the absence of luminal contents, without any apparent stimulus for IPANs to sense, or upon stimulation of nitrergic populations (Nurgali et al., 2004; Koh et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with references to Nurgali et al., 2004; Koh et al., 2022.

claim: CMCs can occur upon stimulation of nitrergic populations.
source: Though IPANs are positioned to initiate motility by activating other subtypes in enteric circuitry, their role in spontaneous CMCs has been debated, as CMCs can occur in the absence of luminal contents, without any apparent stimulus for IPANs to sense, or upon stimulation of nitrergic populations (Nurgali et al., 2004; Koh et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with references to Nurgali et al., 2004; Koh et al., 2022.

claim: IPANs participate in oscillatory rhythmic firing of the ENS during CMCs.
source: Only recently has evidence emerged to suggest that IPANs participate in oscillatory rhythmic firing of the ENS during CMCs, and that activation of neuronal subtypes expressing calretinin, including IPANs, together can evoke CMCs (Hibberd et al., 2018b; Hibberd et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated with references to Hibberd et al., 2018b; Hibberd et al., 2018a.

claim: Activation of neuronal subtypes expressing calretinin, including IPANs, together can evoke CMCs.
source: Only recently has evidence emerged to suggest that IPANs participate in oscillatory rhythmic firing of the ENS during CMCs, and that activation of neuronal subtypes expressing calretinin, including IPANs, together can evoke CMCs (Hibberd et al., 2018b; Hibberd et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated with references to Hibberd et al., 2018b; Hibberd et al., 2018a.

claim: Excitement of IPANs alone in the distal colon is capable of producing retrograde CMCs.
source: Our results demonstrate that excitement of IPANs alone in the distal colon is capable of producing retrograde CMCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the optogenetic data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Failure of proximal colonic stimulation to evoke CMCs may reflect inhibition by IPAN recruitment of descending pathways.
source: Failure of proximal colonic stimulation to evoke CMCs may reflect inhibition by IPAN recruitment of descending pathways; or conversely, high efficacy of stimulation from distal colon may reflect bias toward activation of ascending excitatory cholinergic pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: High efficacy of stimulation from distal colon may reflect bias toward activation of ascending excitatory cholinergic pathways.
source: Failure of proximal colonic stimulation to evoke CMCs may reflect inhibition by IPAN recruitment of descending pathways; or conversely, high efficacy of stimulation from distal colon may reflect bias toward activation of ascending excitatory cholinergic pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: Classification of Cdh6+ neurons as IPANs in the distal colon may not extend to the proximal colon.
source: Our classification of Cdh6+ neurons as IPANs in the distal colon may not extend to the proximal colon; thus, we cannot extrapolate that Cdh6+ optogenetic activation in the colon is restricted to IPANs as in the distal colon.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The stimulus paradigm in the proximal colon may not have activated enough neurons based on light density and illumination.
source: In addition, our stimulus paradigm in the proximal colon may not have activated enough neurons based on light density and illumination.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of calretinin-expressing neurons elicited anterograde CMCs regardless of stimulus location, including proximal colon.
source: In previous studies, optogenetic stimulation of calretinin-expressing neurons or choline acetyl transferase-expressing neurons (both of which include IPANs, interneurons, and motor neurons) elicited anterograde CMCs regardless of stimulus location, including proximal colon (Hibberd et al., 2018a; Efimov et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated with references to Hibberd et al., 2018a; Efimov et al., 2024.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of choline acetyl transferase-expressing neurons elicited anterograde CMCs regardless of stimulus location, including proximal colon.
source: In previous studies, optogenetic stimulation of calretinin-expressing neurons or choline acetyl transferase-expressing neurons (both of which include IPANs, interneurons, and motor neurons) elicited anterograde CMCs regardless of stimulus location, including proximal colon (Hibberd et al., 2018a; Efimov et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated with references to Hibberd et al., 2018a; Efimov et al., 2024.

claim: Proximal colon stimulation of nitric oxide synthase-expressing neurons elicited CMCs.
source: Proximal colon stimulation of nitric oxide synthase-expressing neurons also elicited CMCs (Koh et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Koh et al., 2022.

claim: CMC synchronous firing is dependent on nicotinic cholinergic transmission.
source: Spontaneous and evoked CMCs were abolished in hexamethonium, confirming that CMC synchronous firing is dependent on nicotinic cholinergic transmission (Hibberd et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is confirmed by the hexamethonium experiments shown in Figure 6I, with reference to Hibberd et al., 2018b.

claim: Nicotinic cholinergic transmission is required for greater activation and synchrony of the entire ENS motility network to generate CMCs.
source: This reinforces that nicotinic cholinergic transmission is required for greater activation and synchrony of the entire ENS motility network to generate CMCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hexamethonium experiments shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Slow AHP, IH, and IT have been previously identified as distinguishing characteristics of IPANs in rat and guinea pig.
source: Slow AHP, IH, and IT have been previously identified as distinguishing characteristics of IPANs in rat and guinea pig (Xiao et al., 2004; Nurgali et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with references to Xiao et al., 2004; Nurgali et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2006.

claim: IH and IT have not previously been reported in studies of intact mouse distal colon myenteric plexus due to the conventional reliance on sharp electrode recordings in which voltage clamp is not possible.
source: Although prior studies noted IH and proposed IT in guinea pig Dogiel type II neurons (Nurgali et al., 2007), they have not previously been reported in studies of intact mouse distal colon myenteric plexus due to the conventional reliance on sharp electrode recordings in which voltage clamp is not possible (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with references to Nurgali et al., 2007; Li et al., 2022.

claim: The presence of IH and IT in thalamocortical relay neurons and other cell types supports intrinsic rhythmicity.
source: The presence of IH and IT in thalamocortical relay neurons and other cell types supports intrinsic rhythmicity (McCormick and Pape, 1990; Pape and McCormick, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with references to McCormick and Pape, 1990; Pape and McCormick, 1989.

claim: IH and IT may promote autonomous rhythmic activity in colonic IPANs.
source: It is possible that these two currents may similarly promote autonomous rhythmic activity in colonic IPANs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the presence of IH and IT in colonic IPANs.

claim: IH is conducted through hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels.
source: IH is conducted through hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels (Benarroch, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Benarroch, 2013.

claim: HCN channel family members HCN1 and HCN2 have been shown to be present in mouse distal colonic Dogiel type II neurons.
source: HCN channel family members HCN1 and HCN2 have been shown to be present in mouse distal colonic Dogiel type II neurons (Xiao et al., 2004), and RNA-Seq ENS screens similarly indicate their expression in IPANs (Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with references to Xiao et al., 2004; Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021.

claim: RNA-Seq ENS screens indicate HCN1 and HCN2 expression in IPANs.
source: HCN channel family members HCN1 and HCN2 have been shown to be present in mouse distal colonic Dogiel type II neurons (Xiao et al., 2004), and RNA-Seq ENS screens similarly indicate their expression in IPANs (Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with references to Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021.

claim: Knockout of HCN2 in mouse leads to a severe growth restriction phenotype due to malnutrition and GI dysmotility.
source: Knockout of HCN2 in mouse leads to a severe growth restriction phenotype due to malnutrition and GI dysmotility (Fisher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Fisher et al., 2018.

claim: Pharmacologic blockade of IH with two distinct HCN channel blockers ZD7288 and CsCl abolishes CMCs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that pharmacologic blockade of IH, which we show to be present in IPANs, with two distinct HCN channel blockers ZD7288 and CsCl abolishes CMCs, an otherwise persistent and ongoing pattern of motor activity in the mouse colon.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 6J-K.

claim: IH in colonic IPANs may play a role in promoting either rhythmic oscillatory single neuron activity or network burst firing, or both.
source: We speculate that IH in colonic IPANs, as in thalamocortical neurons, plays a role in promoting either rhythmic oscillatory single neuron activity or network burst firing, or both (McCormick and Pape, 1990; Pape and McCormick, 1989).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the pharmacological data and comparison to thalamocortical neurons, with references to McCormick and Pape, 1990; Pape and McCormick, 1989.

claim: Blocking IH may impair individual IPANs' ability to fire rhythmically.
source: Blocking IH may impair individual IPANs' ability to fire rhythmically, or the ability of IPANs to synchronize into a network burst firing mode.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the effects of IH blockade.

claim: Blocking IH may impair the ability of IPANs to synchronize into a network burst firing mode.
source: Blocking IH may impair individual IPANs' ability to fire rhythmically, or the ability of IPANs to synchronize into a network burst firing mode.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the effects of IH blockade.

claim: Failure of IPANs to fully activate and synchronize could prevent generation of synchronized rhythmic myenteric network activation of motility circuits.
source: Failure of IPANs to fully activate and synchronize could prevent generation of both (Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020) synchronized rhythmic myenteric network activation of motility circuits, and (Nurgali et al., 2004) the resulting synchronized contractions that sum to much larger contractile forces during CMCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the effects of IH blockade, with references to Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020; Nurgali et al., 2004.

claim: Failure of IPANs to fully activate and synchronize could prevent generation of synchronized contractions that sum to much larger contractile forces during CMCs.
source: Failure of IPANs to fully activate and synchronize could prevent generation of both (Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020) synchronized rhythmic myenteric network activation of motility circuits, and (Nurgali et al., 2004) the resulting synchronized contractions that sum to much larger contractile forces during CMCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the effects of IH blockade, with references to Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020; Nurgali et al., 2004.

claim: Type II cadherins are most commonly homophilic synaptic cell adhesion molecules.
source: Type II cadherins are most commonly homophilic synaptic cell adhesion molecules (Yamagata et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with references to Yamagata et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2015.

claim: Cdh6 can also form heterodimers with Cdh7, Cdh10, and Cdh14.
source: Cdh6 can also form heterodimers with Cdh7, Cdh10, and Cdh14 (Shimoyama et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Shimoyama et al., 2000.

claim: Cdh10 and Cdh14 are very lowly expressed in the colon by single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: However, Cdh10 and Cdh14 are very lowly expressed in the colon by single-cell RNA sequencing (Drokhlyansky et al., 2020), and we performed RNAscope for Cdh7 and did not observe any expression (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Drokhlyansky et al., 2020, and based on experimental observations.

claim: RNAscope for Cdh7 did not show any expression in the colon.
source: However, Cdh10 and Cdh14 are very lowly expressed in the colon by single-cell RNA sequencing (Drokhlyansky et al., 2020), and we performed RNAscope for Cdh7 and did not observe any expression (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Restricted expression of Cdh6 and Cdh8 to mouse colonic IPANs raises the possibility of these cadherins supporting IPAN-IPAN synaptic connections.
source: Restricted expression of two type II cadherins, Cdh6 and Cdh8, to mouse colonic IPANs raises the possibility of these cadherins supporting IPAN-IPAN synaptic connections.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the expression pattern of Cdh6 and Cdh8.

claim: IPANs are not known to receive synaptic input and have been characterized electrophysiologically by their lack thereof.
source: While broadly speaking, IPANs are not known to receive synaptic input and in fact have been characterized electrophysiologically by their lack thereof (Hirst et al., 1974), some work has in fact suggested that AH-AH neuron interconnected pairs may exist (Kunze et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with references to Hirst et al., 1974; Kunze et al., 1993.

claim: Some work has suggested that AH-AH neuron interconnected pairs may exist.
source: While broadly speaking, IPANs are not known to receive synaptic input and in fact have been characterized electrophysiologically by their lack thereof (Hirst et al., 1974), some work has in fact suggested that AH-AH neuron interconnected pairs may exist (Kunze et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Kunze et al., 1993.

claim: Calbindin-positive neurons, presumed IPANs, do receive synapses, though fewer than non-calbindin neurons.
source: Immunohistochemical and electron microscopy investigation of synapses on enteric neurons further showed that calbindin-positive neurons, presumed IPANs, do receive synapses, though fewer than non-calbindin neurons, and some of those synapses were also calbindin-reactive (Pompolo and Furness, 1988).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Pompolo and Furness, 1988.

claim: Some synapses on calbindin-positive neurons were also calbindin-reactive.
source: Immunohistochemical and electron microscopy investigation of synapses on enteric neurons further showed that calbindin-positive neurons, presumed IPANs, do receive synapses, though fewer than non-calbindin neurons, and some of those synapses were also calbindin-reactive (Pompolo and Furness, 1988).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Pompolo and Furness, 1988.

claim: An 'IPAN driver circuit' theory proposes that IPANs form an interconnected network of positive feedback to synchronize and amplify sensory signaling.
source: These observations informed a proposed 'IPAN driver circuit' theory, in which IPANs form an interconnected network of positive feedback to synchronize and amplify sensory signaling and thus activate large swaths of enteric circuitry (Wood, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Wood, 2012.

claim: Activation of large regions of the ENS has been suggested to be driven by interneuronal networks.
source: In contrast, more recently, activation of large regions of the ENS has been suggested to be driven by interneuronal networks (Barth et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Barth et al., 2022.

claim: The study was unsuccessful in localizing Cdh6 protein via immunohistochemistry.
source: It is important to note that our study was unsuccessful in localizing Cdh6 protein via immunohistochemistry, to confirm protein expression in neurons or in Cdh6-cre-tdT+ muscle cells or visualize synaptic connections between neurons or connections to other cell types.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Intrinsic sensory neurons are an essential part of the enteric nervous system (ENS).
source: Intrinsic sensory neurons are an essential part of the enteric nervous system (ENS) and play a crucial role in gastrointestinal tract motility and digestion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Intrinsic sensory neurons play a crucial role in gastrointestinal tract motility and digestion.
source: Intrinsic sensory neurons are an essential part of the enteric nervous system (ENS) and play a crucial role in gastrointestinal tract motility and digestion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Neuronal subtypes in the ENS have been distinguished by their electrophysiological properties, morphology, and expression of characteristic markers, notably neurotransmitters and neuropeptides.
source: Neuronal subtypes in the ENS have been distinguished by their electrophysiological properties, morphology, and expression of characteristic markers, notably neurotransmitters and neuropeptides.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: The GI tract is the only internal organ system containing its own sensory neurons.
source: The GI tract is the only internal organ system containing its own sensory neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) detect relevant stimuli through chemo- and mechano-sensation.
source: Intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) detect relevant stimuli through chemo- and mechano-sensation and direct appropriate GI functions via downstream components of the enteric nervous system (ENS), including ascending and descending interneurons, and excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons (Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020.

claim: IPANs direct appropriate GI functions via downstream components of the ENS, including ascending and descending interneurons, and excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons.
source: Intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) detect relevant stimuli through chemo- and mechano-sensation and direct appropriate GI functions via downstream components of the enteric nervous system (ENS), including ascending and descending interneurons, and excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons (Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020.

claim: Enteric neuronal subtypes have begun to be distinguished morphologically, electrophysiologically, and by marker expression, classically especially of neurotransmitters.
source: These neuronal subtypes have begun to be distinguished morphologically, electrophysiologically, and by marker expression, classically especially of neurotransmitters (Nurgali et al., 2004; Qu et al., 2008), and together this information has provided an opening to characterize individual neuron subtype function within the GI tract.
evidence: This is stated with references to Nurgali et al., 2004; Qu et al., 2008.

claim: Type II cadherins are a family of synaptic cell adhesion molecules with combinatorial expression in multiple neural circuits of the CNS.
source: Type II cadherins are a family of synaptic cell adhesion molecules with combinatorial expression in multiple neural circuits of the CNS, including retina, limbic, olivonuclear, and auditory projection systems (Suzuki et al., 1997; Duan et al., 2018; Honjo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with references to Suzuki et al., 1997; Duan et al., 2018; Honjo et al., 2000.

claim: Type II cadherins bind homophilically by expression of the same cadherin at both the pre- and post-synapse.
source: Type II cadherins bind homophilically by expression of the same cadherin at both the pre- and post-synapse, which stabilizes developing synapses between correct partners while incorrect synapses are pruned away (Yamagata et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with references to Yamagata et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2015.

claim: Type II cadherin binding stabilizes developing synapses between correct partners while incorrect synapses are pruned away.
source: Type II cadherins bind homophilically by expression of the same cadherin at both the pre- and post-synapse, which stabilizes developing synapses between correct partners while incorrect synapses are pruned away (Yamagata et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with references to Yamagata et al., 2018; Basu et al., 2015.

claim: Recent RNA-Seq studies of human and mouse ENS have identified synaptic cell adhesion molecules, including type II cadherins, expressed in enteric neuronal subtypes.
source: Recent RNA-Seq studies of human and mouse ENS have identified synaptic cell adhesion molecules, including type II cadherins, expressed in enteric neuronal subtypes (May-Zhang et al., 2021; Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with references to May-Zhang et al., 2021; Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021.

claim: The specificity of type II cadherin expression has yet to be harnessed to assess neuronal subtype-specific function in the ENS.
source: However, the specificity of their expression has yet to be harnessed to assess neuronal subtype-specific function in the ENS.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claim: IH is a rhythmicity indicator in thalamocortical and other systems.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of sensory neurons in situ reveal action potential (AP) slow afterhyperpolarizations characteristic of IPANs, and hyperpolarization-activated cationic current (IH), a rhythmicity indicator in thalamocortical and other systems (Wahl-Schott and Biel, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Wahl-Schott and Biel, 2009.

claim: During CMCs, large regions of the ENS oscillate in synchrony at 1–2 Hz to generate traveling contractions along the colon.
source: During CMCs, large regions of the ENS oscillate in synchrony at 1–2 Hz to generate traveling contractions along the colon (Spencer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Spencer et al., 2021.

claim: Recent calcium imaging studies have shown that IPANs participate, along with all other subtypes of enteric neurons, in synchronized oscillatory firing during CMCs.
source: Recent calcium imaging studies have shown that IPANs participate, along with all other subtypes of enteric neurons, in this synchronized oscillatory firing (Hibberd et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Hibberd et al., 2018b.

claim: In thalamocortical relay neurons, IH contributes to intrinsic slow rhythmic burst firing at 1–2 Hz.
source: In thalamocortical relay neurons, IH contributes to intrinsic slow rhythmic burst firing at 1–2 Hz (McCormick and Pape, 1990), but the function of IH in colonic IPANs is not known.
evidence: This is stated with reference to McCormick and Pape, 1990.

claim: The function of IH in colonic IPANs is not known.
source: In thalamocortical relay neurons, IH contributes to intrinsic slow rhythmic burst firing at 1–2 Hz (McCormick and Pape, 1990), but the function of IH in colonic IPANs is not known.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: The role of IPANs in spontaneous CMCs is not well understood.
source: However, the role of IPANs in spontaneous CMCs is not well understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.
